claims.summary: The training identifies input capacity and latency as selection constraints. Under the supplied accounting rule, 800 + 4×1100 + 700 = 5900 tokens fits G2, and E2 plus G2 takes 90 + 600 = 690 ms within 750 ms. This is an anonymous planning fixture, not a named model capability or production percentile guarantee.

G2 accepts the stipulated 5900-token envelope, but E1 plus G2 requires 800 ms and fails the 750 ms budget. This pairing could satisfy a task allowing at least 800 ms; adequate context capacity alone does not satisfy both independent constraints.

E2/G1 totals 490 ms but G1 has only a 4096-token window. It would fit a smaller permitted context envelope, whereas the current task prohibits removing required context or output reserve. The source supports considering token limits, not these hypothetical numbers.

The 600 ms latency is acceptable, but the same G1 window still fails the 5900-token requirement. This would be feasible with a smaller complete token envelope; no additional architecture or unstated performance tradeoff needs to be invented.

The frozen local ONNX example separately enables PREVIEW_FEATURES and the server's external AI runtime setting. Correct paths alone leave the explicitly disabled server runtime unchanged. This plan could suffice if that setting were already enabled, which is not the supplied setup.

The actual local example is Windows-only, requires installed Machine Learning Services and ONNX Runtime 1.19 or later, and defines the remaining runtime switch and path roles. With those prerequisites now explicitly supplied, LOCATION identifies the model directory and LOCAL_RUNTIME_PATH identifies the runtime-library directory.

The reference assigns model.onnx/tokenizer.json to LOCATION's directory and runtime libraries to LOCAL_RUNTIME_PATH. Swapping those directories violates the supplied inventory. It could work only if their contents and roles were changed to match, a different configuration from this fixture.

The local model registration example expressly points LOCATION at the directory containing the model and tokenizer artifacts. An individual-file LOCATION would need a different documented interface; it is not the stated local ONNX contract. No filename repair or live runtime behavior is inferred from the article's inconsistent later tokenizer spelling.

The cited operations produce relevance signals, not enforcement of current Boolean stock or market predicates. Embedding those labels could aid a descriptive task, but cannot replace the hard relational eligibility rule specified here.

A filter after ordered TOP acts only on rows that survived that limit. It can enforce a final display rule when underfilled pools are acceptable, but it cannot satisfy the explicit condition that ineligible rows consume no earlier branch budget.

Filtering each exact-vector and full-text branch before its own ordered cap implements the supplied eligibility contract while retaining both ranking signals. The hybrid training and TOP query-scope contract support this placement; no Preview approximate-index filtering behavior is invoked.

Fusion can retain candidates appearing only in the vector branch, so restricting only lexical results leaves an unrestricted entry path. One-sided filtering could fit an independently prefiltered other branch, but the alternative explicitly leaves it unrestricted here.

Recreating an index over unchanged vectors does not regenerate their semantic content. Rebuilding can address format migration or a large changed vector distribution, but the stipulated defect is the unchanged old-text vector itself.

ALLOW_STALE_VECTOR_INDEX addresses writes with earlier formats when stale search is tolerated. That can be relevant to an older index's write policy, not the already enabled latest-format index or the missing text-to-vector generation step in this scenario.

A distance metric compares supplied vectors and does not recompute them from modified source text. A different validated similarity objective could warrant changing metrics, but cannot repair the stated missing embedding refresh.

The maintenance and generation sources separate producing a vector from indexing its value. Regenerating from the new Body and persisting that vector supplies the actual changed indexed value. This remains a bounded layer diagnosis, not a guarantee of exactly-once workers or search relevance.

The reference explains that schema-first import attempts vector-index creation before loading the required vectors. Keeping ordinary schema objects in an import can be appropriate, but later generation cannot repair this earlier vector-index creation failure.

The documented workaround excludes the vector index from the import artifact and recreates it after data loading. The separate threshold is at least 100 nonnull vectors. Those two requirements, with the supplied valid key and supported Preview region, identify this plan.

The threshold counts nonnull vectors, not total table rows, so the supplied 95 values are insufficient. This plan becomes feasible after at least five additional valid vector values have been populated, not merely because the table has 130 rows.

Creating this index on an empty target violates its required population at creation time. Empty-table index creation is familiar for conventional indexes, but is not the documented Preview vector-index prerequisite.

K2 shares two and three IDs with the respective exact five-neighbor lists, so its mean recall is 0.5. Its 35 ms p95 is fast enough but cannot compensate for the 0.8 recall floor. It could qualify only under a different accepted recall requirement.

Exact search supplies the reference neighbor sets and has recall one against that baseline, but its stipulated 110 ms p95 exceeds 90 ms. It could be selected with a relaxed budget or separately demonstrated faster execution; no universal crossover is assumed.

M7 reproduces both exact lists in this fixture but its 95 ms p95 misses the hard latency gate. It could satisfy a different latency budget. Its perfect overlap on these two lists is not a general claim of perfect ANN recall.

R4 shares four of five exact neighbors for each query, so mean recall is 0.8, and 75 ms meets the independent latency bound. The opaque label has no capability meaning; the supplied measurements, common snapshot/filter/metric and documented recall definition determine the answer.
